intro.kicker: A short history of Swedish candy
title: From polkagris
to pick-n-mix

footnotes.1: Polkagris / Amalia Eriksson: SKBL, Tekniska museet
footnotes.3: US cinema snacks: Smithsonian; UCL thesis
footnotes.8: Pastellfiskar / Swedish Fish: Cloetta, Wikipedia, Mental Floss

story.text: The first candies were medicinal in nature. Sugar was used to disguise the bad taste of a concoction of herbs prescribed by an apothecary for things like digestion issues and chest pain.

In the 1850s in Sweden a widow called Amalia Eriksson invented a famous candy called polkagris. Polkagris is a red and white striped peppermint stick. The candy was first made for her sick daughter to help with a cold. It was made of sugar, peppermint, water, and vinegar. Soon after, she started selling them in her bakery. She died at age 99 a very wealthy woman because of the bestselling candy.[1]

Once candy became less about curing ailments and more for pleasure, it was only the rich that could afford to buy it. A sign of a well-to-do home was to have bonbons in little bowls ready for guests. In the 1850s railways in Sweden and the rest of the world made sugar and other ingredients cheaper. This meant that ordinary people and not just the rich could afford to buy candy.
Once factories were able to make candy it became a real industry as one factory could make more in a day than a shop could make in months.

Between about 1900 and 1930, electric motors replaced steam engines. Every machine could now run on its own, so factories set them up in a line from the cooking pot to the wrapper, with conveyor belts carrying candy between them and machines doing the wrapping. Cleaner, faster factories made candy even cheaper.

Cinemas spread fast in Sweden in the early 1900s and by 1916 there were about 500.[2] In the 1930s, US cinemas found that selling candy and popcorn helped them survive hard times, and candy became a ritual of going to the movies.[3]

When the Great Depression hit in 1929, money got tight around the world, but candy held on. A small sweet was one of the few treats people could still afford. In the US, candy makers sold bigger, more filling bars for a nickel, almost as a cheap meal. Snickers (1930) and 3 Musketeers (1932) both date from those years.

Sweden felt the slump later and less sharply, and it recovered faster than the US in the mid-1930s. Swedish candy makers kept going by selling cheap, everyday sweets, like loose candies sold one by one for a coin or two.

photos.alt: Ration card for coffee and tea, 1945

story.text: Sugar was rationed during the Second World War, from April 1940 to September 1949, which made making candy difficult.[4] With sugar rationed and cocoa nearly impossible to import, chocolate became scarce and factories used substitutes, made fewer products and sometimes paused lines. Sweets were a rare treat for kids growing up in those years. Sugar rationing lasted past the war, ending in the 1940s. The pent-up demand helped set off the candy boom of the 1950s.

In the 1940s the Swedish government wanted to find out what was causing cavities in the Swedish people. From 1945 to 1955, the government ran studies to find out the cause. The tests showed that sticky sweets, eaten often, cause tooth decay.[5] Health officials ran a campaign to tell parents to give children sweets on just one day a week. That became lördagsgodis, which means "Saturday sweets."[6] Today, Saturday is still the big day for sweets in Sweden for not just children but adults too.

After the war, sugar was no longer rationed, wages were rising, and families had a little extra money to spend. Candy factories could turn out sweets faster and cheaper than ever. New methods like pouring candy into shapes pressed into trays of cornstarch made soft, chewy gummies and foam sweets easy to mass-produce.

Cars were the other big symbol of the era. Many Swedish families bought their first car in the 1950s. In 1953, Ahlgren's in Gävle launched Ahlgrens bilar, which means "Ahlgren's cars": little foam candies shaped like cars, in pink, green and white. Cloetta, which makes them today, still calls them "the world's best-selling car."[7]

Around the late 1950s, the Swedish candy maker Malaco created a small, chewy red fish to sell in North America. The fish shape was a nod to Sweden's fishing industry. In the US and Canada they became famous as Swedish Fish, and back home Swedes came to know them as pastellfiskar, or "pastel fish." Today they're probably the best-known Swedish candy in the world.[8]
The 1960s were when Swedish candy got playful. With money and sugar plentiful, makers stopped focusing on cheap basics and started competing on fun shapes, bright colours and new textures.

items.text: Haribo launched its Nappar in 1961, and sour cola versions came later.[9]
Cloetta made its first marshmallow Santas in the 1960s[10], and foam sweets in all kinds of shapes became shop staples.
postwar children had their own spending money, and makers designed candy straight for them with animals, cars and cartoons.

story.text: In 1979 Malaco invented the concept of Gott & Blandat, which means "good and mixed." It was a way of selling leftover candies they had by creating mixed bags of fruit gums and licorice.[11]

Until now, loose sweets were sold from behind a counter. In 1985 the state food agency said shops could let people pick their own from bins.[12] That is lösgodis, Swedish for loose sweets, better known as pick-and-mix. It fit the times, as self-service shops and big supermarkets spread.
The bins filled with staples that are still there today: a candy fried egg, strawberries, cherries, orange discs, and Rambo.

In 1992 the Lindström family in Huskvarna, near Jönköping, put their house up as security for a bank loan. They used it to buy their first candy machine and started BUBS, a family candy maker. The name comes from four of them: Bernt, Ulrik, Birgitta and Stefan. They chose bold shapes such as skulls, ovals and diamonds.[13]
In 2010 Stefan Ernberg and Florence Baras opened Sockerbit, a Swedish candy shop in New York, on Christopher Street in the West Village. In 2014 Sockerbit opened a second shop, in Los Angeles.[14]

story.text: The pandemic began in 2020, and TikTok became a main way people found new things to buy. In January 2024 a TikTok video set off a craze for Swedish candy in the US. Chewy skull-shaped sweets led the way, many of them made by BUBS. Shops ran short, and some sweets were hard to find.[15]
